name: Enoch Powell
role: British Conservative then Ulster Unionist MP, Minister of Health (1960–63)
summary: Powell was a free-market, monetarist Conservative who held that Parliament is the sole sovereign authority, opposing Lords reform, a bill of rights, devolution and British membership of the European Community. He called for ending Commonwealth immigration and for assisted re-emigration, and later sat for the Ulster Unionists, opposing nuclear weapons and defending the established Church of England.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: In the Budget debate of 21 April 1969 (col. 94) he set the Government's view that it knows the right pattern of activity against his own side's view that the right pattern is that freely chosen through the price and market mechanism with as little distortion as possible.

central-planning.rationale: In the same 21 April 1969 Budget speech (col. 94) he rejected the view that the right economic pattern is whatever Government judges right, endorsing free choice through price and profit instead.

state-directs-investment.rationale: In the 21 April 1969 Budget speech (col. 94) he argued against Government deciding the pattern of economic activity and for the price and profit mechanism, and on 24 June 1969 (col. 1395) called Government-induced distortions of resource use worse than unnecessary.

public-ownership.rationale: On 18 February 1960 (Iron and Steel Bill, col. 1472) he hoped capital for steel would not interfere with the earliest practicable denationalisation of Richard Thomas and Baldwin's, welcoming private ownership as part of the private enterprise system.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: On 30 November 1976 (col. 758) he called the public sector borrowing requirement exorbitant and said it had to be cut to what voluntary savings could finance; on 14 November 1974 (col. 672) he ascribed inflation to excessive monetary expansion and backed control of public spending.

price-controls-fight-inflation.rationale: On 14 November 1974 (col. 672) he said he had long held that inflation derives from a single monetary cause, the excessive expansion of monetary demand, which leaves no role for price controls as a cure.

free-trade.rationale: On 26 June 1986 (col. 554) he said the European Community's external restrictions had disastrously interfered with trade with the outside world and that many wondered whether that damage outweighed the gains from its internal free market.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: On 26 June 1986 (col. 554) he criticised the Community's external trade restrictions as damaging; on 30 November 1976 (col. 758) he said there was no case for import controls as a remedy for the borrowing requirement.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: In the Family Income Supplements Bill debate of 10 November 1970 (col. 260) he read out Trevelyan's account of the Speenhamland system of topping up wages from the rates, with its consequences of pauperising the labourer, as a warning against the Bill.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: On 11 March 1986 (col. 889) he complained that the Northern Ireland appropriation procedure gave no real scrutiny of separate items of expenditure by Members, and in the 1984 and 1985 Northern Ireland funding debates he pressed for proper House control of spending.

parliament-supreme.rationale: On 7 July 1975 (col. 47) he held that an entrenched Bill of Rights is incompatible with the responsibility of Government through the House to the electorate, and on 4 December 1975 (Civil List Bill, col. 1988) he said this Parliament, unlike a legislature bound by a treaty or text, is sovereign.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: On 7 July 1975 (United Kingdom Bill of Rights, col. 47) he argued that a Bill of Rights as an entrenched protection of rights is incompatible with the British constitution and with the House's responsibility to the electorate.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: On 17 February 1972 (European Communities Bill, col. 698) and on 4 and 6 December 1975 he opposed the overriding authority of the Community over this country and said an elected European Parliament could never be sovereign as this Parliament was; Britannica notes his opposition to entry into the EEC.

national-law-over-international.rationale: On 17 February 1972 (col. 698) he objected to Community law becoming part of British law with overriding authority, and on 4 December 1975 (col. 1988) said above a Community assembly there would always be a sovereign treaty text that it could not amend, unlike this Parliament.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: On 4 December 1975 (Civil List Bill, col. 1988) he said the country is perhaps the only one with a true monarchy, acting on the advice of those who are responsible in this House, and defended the institution.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: On 12 February 1969 (Exclusion of Peers by Succession, col. 1351) he defended the hereditary basis of the House of Lords against the Government's Bill, and on 19 February 1969 (col. 503) attacked the plan for a two-tier chamber of voting and non-voting peers.

second-chamber.rationale: On 19 February 1969 (col. 503) and 12 February 1969 (col. 1351) he defended the existing House of Lords and opposed replacing it with a reformed two-tier chamber, valuing it as a traditional second chamber.

proportional-representation.rationale: On 7 March 1985 (Northern Ireland local elections, col. 1202) he called proportional representation foisted on the Province and unacceptable, and on 21 January 1985 (col. 827) called it a 'curse'.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: On 20 July 1978 (col. 864) he argued that in a unitary State legislative power cannot be divided between this House and another Assembly, treating devolved powers as held within Parliament's sovereignty.

national-church-status.rationale: On 24 February 1986 (Bishops (Retirement) Measure, col. 775) he defended the established status of the Church of England as a valuable and durable institution.

separate-church-state.rationale: On 24 February 1986 (col. 775) he defended the established status of the Church of England against Tony Benn's attack on it, calling it a valuable and durable institution.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: On 28 October 1986 (Deacons (Ordination of Women) Measure, col. 208) he said the House exercises the function of a legislature for the Church of England, with a duty to make sound law for it.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: On 24 February 1986 (col. 775) he said it is no bad thing to recognise institutions that are valuable and durable though they express widespread prejudice and cannot be demonstrated necessary, naming the established Church; on 12 February 1969 (col. 1351) he defended the Lords on its historical growth.

reduce-immigration.rationale: In the Birmingham speech of 20 April 1968 he said the total inflow for settlement should be reduced at once to negligible proportions and called for stopping, or virtually stopping, further inflow; Britannica likewise reports his call for voluntary repatriation.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: In the 20 April 1968 speech he opposed the Race Relations Bill and the demand for legislation against discrimination, saying the citizen should not be denied his right to discriminate in the management of his own affairs between one fellow-citizen and another.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: In the 20 April 1968 speech he said all who are in this country as citizens should be equal before the law, with no discrimination or difference made between them by public authority, while opposing anti-discrimination legislation.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: In the 20 April 1968 speech he said that where there are marked physical differences, especially of colour, integration is difficult, and that growing forces were acting against integration of the immigrant communities.

former-empire-equal-treatment.rationale: On 11 July 1973 (col. 1734) he said the franchise should attach to citizenship in the narrower and proper sense, not to Commonwealth status, as in any other country, and in the 20 April 1968 speech he treated Commonwealth citizens and aliens alike as to entry for settlement.

death-penalty.rationale: On 26 November 1975 (Prevention of Terrorism Bill, col. 919) he said his conviction was that the death penalty would not deter terrorism but stimulate it, while distinguishing that from the penalty for murder in general.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: On 28 June 1983 (col. 494), 24 May 1984 (col. 1331) he argued that no circumstance could make it to Britain's advantage to use a nuclear weapon and that the deterrent rationale could not rationally be made good.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: On 24 May 1984 (col. 1331) he rejected the proposition that nuclear weapons are needed for deterrence, and on 28 June 1983 (col. 494) argued that using Polaris or Trident would ensure Britain's destruction.
